- **Strengths**: Prevents high-frequency artifacts early in training; stabilizes optimization for deformable scenes; reduces local minima [S1, S4].

The claim consists of three parts: 1) Prevents high-frequency artifacts early in training, 2) Stabilizes optimization for deformable scenes, and 3) Reduces local minima. Source [S1] explicitly states that training without annealing leads to 'noisy normal maps' (high-frequency artifacts) and that noise at high frequencies 'hardly converges,' implying the annealing strategy prevents this. Source [S4] describes a 'coarse-to-fine deformation regularization' that eases in high frequencies, noting that 'large motions are a main source of local minima' and that disabling this regularization causes significant performance drops for dynamic (deformable) scenes, thereby supporting the claims that the method stabilizes optimization and reduces local minima.

Equivalent to rho in [S3, unofficial] or alpha in [S9].

The claim states that the parameter rho in [S3] is equivalent to alpha in [S9]. Source [S3] defines rho as a scheduling variable that linearly increases from 0 to L (number of frequency bases) to gradually activate frequency bands. Source [S9] describes alpha as a parameter that linearly increases from 0 to m (number of frequencies) to slide a window function over frequency bands. Both sources explicitly link these parameters to the same coarse-to-fine optimization strategy using windowed positional encodings (citing Park et al. [2020] in both contexts). The mathematical definitions of the windowing functions and the role of the parameters are consistent across both sources, supporting the equivalence.

This aligns with the claim that the landscape is smoothed (by suppressing high frequencies) and allows the network to learn coarse geometry before refining details.

It solves the problem of optimization instability and local minima caused by high-frequency details appearing too early, which leads to artifacts like self-occlusions or incorrect geometry [S1, S4][S6, unofficial].

The claim states that the method solves optimization instability and local minima caused by high-frequency details appearing too early, which leads to artifacts like self-occlusions or incorrect geometry. Source [S1] explicitly mentions that initially generated noise at high PE frequencies becomes hard to manipulate and hardly converges to correct geometry, and that annealing alleviates this. Source [S4] notes that large motions create many local minima and that coarse-to-fine regularization helps avoid performance drops associated with these local minima. Source [S6] explicitly states that high-frequency occlusions (self-occlusions) can fill space and that the coarse-to-fine frequency annealing strategy suppresses this by forcing the network to optimize low-frequency details first, minimizing self-occlusions and easing the optimization difficulty. All specific facts in the claim are present in the provided evidence.
